runtime_boundary: Represents the generate() API layer published as onnxruntime-genai, not ONNX Runtime itself, which is the general-purpose ONNX inference engine and execution-provider framework underneath it. Products that embed this library, including Foundry Local, Windows ML, and the Visual Studio Code AI Toolkit, are separate boundaries. The library has no server, no network endpoint, and no graphical interface; it is exercised through host application code, which places it on the runtime side of the ADR 015 runtime-versus-assistant test as an embedded library rather than an assistant.
model_management: Models are ONNX directories containing a genai_config.json alongside graph and tokenizer assets, loaded from a local path; a model-package layout can bundle several hardware variants of one model and select at load time. The repository ships a model builder that converts and quantizes Hugging Face PyTorch, quantized PyTorch, and GGUF sources into the required ONNX layout, and the project documents downloading prebuilt ONNX models through the Hugging Face CLI or Foundry Local. There is no runtime model store, registry, or removal command; LoRA adapters use a documented .onnx_adapter flatbuffers file and multi-adapter switching.
hardware_requirements: The project's support matrix documents Linux, Windows, macOS, and Android on x86, x64, and arm64, with CPU, CUDA, DirectML, NvTensorRtRtx, OpenVINO, QNN, and WebGPU acceleration; AMD GPU support is listed as roadmap. Qualcomm Snapdragon NPU execution requires the separate onnxruntime-qnn execution-provider plugin and a model packaged with compiled QNN graph artifacts, and Python, C, C++, and C# are supported while Java requires a source build.
operational_controls: Search, sampling, and KV-cache behaviour are configured through genai_config.json and per-generator search options; provider options such as the Qualcomm HTP performance mode are set on the model configuration. Runtime options can terminate and restart a generation session and toggle ONNX Runtime profiling per token during generation.
strengths: One generation loop targets CPU, CUDA, DirectML, and Qualcomm NPU hardware across Windows, Linux, macOS, and Android from Python, C, C++, C#, and Java bindings.
Constrained decoding through LLGuidance provides Lark grammar, JSON schema, and regex outputs for tool calling, alongside multi-LoRA adapters with a published adapter file specification.
The repository documents a paged-attention engine with continuous batching, and both draft-model and n-gram speculative decoding, with explicit statements of their limits.
tradeoffs: Execution is limited to ONNX graphs, so any other weight format must first be converted with the model builder or Olive, and per-execution-provider artifacts such as QNN context binaries are built separately.
There is no server, endpoint, authentication, metrics, or health surface; only in-process profiling and logging, so operational visibility depends entirely on the host application.

The continuous-batching Engine API is documented as a transitional host-facing surface that is not thread-safe, and the published support matrix still lists speculative decoding as roadmap while the repository documents it as implemented, so capability varies by version and build.
license_note: The repository publishes a single MIT license file covering the generate() API implementation. A ThirdPartyNotices.txt file lists the licenses of bundled dependencies and does not restrict or alter the project's own MIT terms.
